sections.heading: Electrical Repair in Wichita: Start With What You're Seeing
body: Most electrical problems give a warning long before anything fails. Here's what the common signs usually point to.

items.title: A breaker that keeps tripping
items.text: Usually an overloaded circuit, a short or a ground fault. Resetting it over and over doesn't fix any of the three.

items.title: An outlet or switch plate that feels warm
items.text: A loose connection can heat up behind the plate. Stop using it and have it looked at.

items.title: Lights that flicker or dim
items.text: Often a loose connection somewhere on the circuit, or a large appliance starting up on the same line.

items.title: Outlets that quit working
items.text: A tripped GFCI somewhere else, a loose wire or a failed device. The cause isn't always at the dead outlet.

items.title: Something fixed before is acting up again
items.text: The part may have been replaced without the cause being found. Tell us what was done, and we start from there.

tail: Each of these starts with a phone call about what you're seeing.

sections.heading: What Usually Causes It
body: The same handful of causes sit behind most calls. Knowing them helps you describe the problem, and tells you when to stop using something.

items.title: A breaker that trips again and again
items.text: An overloaded circuit, a short or a ground fault. A breaker is doing its job when it trips. Resetting it repeatedly hides the reason.

items.title: A dead outlet
items.text: Often a tripped GFCI on another outlet, a loose wire behind the plate or a failed receptacle. A garage, bathroom or outdoor outlet may be fed from a different spot than you'd guess.

items.title: A plate that feels warm
items.text: Heat at an outlet or switch usually means a loose or worn connection. Stop using it, keep things unplugged and have it looked at soon.

items.title: Flickering or dimming lights
items.text: A loose connection on the circuit, or a big load such as a compressor starting on the same line. A single room points one direction, the whole house another.

items.title: Buzzing, crackling or a burnt smell
items.text: These are stop signs. Switch off the circuit if you can do it safely and call. If you see smoke or flames, leave and call 911.

items.title: A repair that didn't hold
items.text: Usually the part was replaced and the cause stayed. Tell us what was done and when it came back.

sections.quote: Quick response. Excellent knowledge and service.
sections.name: CE U.

sections.heading: Repair, or Something Bigger?
body: Many electrical repairs are small: a device, a connection, a breaker. Older homes sometimes show more. Wiring laid out for far fewer appliances than a house has today can run out of room, and a house that's been added onto may have wiring from several eras.
When what we find is bigger than a repair, we say so, explain what we saw and lay out your options. You'll never need to guess whether the answer is a repair or a rewire.

sections.heading: Before You Call
body: A few minutes of notes make the call faster. Write down which outlets or rooms are affected, whether a breaker tripped, what was running at the time, and whether anyone has worked on it before.

If you can do it safely, leave the affected circuit off and unplug what was on it. Don't keep resetting a breaker that keeps tripping. If a plate is hot or something smells burnt, switch the circuit off and call.

sections.heading: Houses, Rentals and Businesses
body: We do electrical repair for homes first, and for offices, shops and other commercial buildings too. If you manage a rental or a family member's house, tell us who will be there and how to reach them, and we'll plan around it.
Residential and commercial work both come through the same number, and a call is the quickest way to get on the schedule.

items.q: What should I tell you when I call?
items.a: What it's doing, where, and since when. Which breaker trips, which outlets are dead, whether a plate is warm. Mention anything someone already tried.

items.q: Is a warm outlet an emergency?
items.a: Treat it as one until it's looked at. Stop using it and unplug what's on it. If you see smoke, smell burning or see scorch marks, leave and call 911.

items.q: Can you work in a garage or a shed?
items.a: Yes. Outlets and wiring in a garage or outbuilding are part of residential service work.

items.q: Do you repair commercial buildings too?
items.a: Yes. We work on offices, restaurants, churches and clinics, as well as homes.
It depends on the cause, so we won't print a number. Ask on the call, and decide before the work starts.

sections.heading: How Outdoor Wiring Is Different
body: Outdoor electrical gets rain, ice and a Kansas summer. Fixtures need to be rated for outdoor use, connections need to be sealed, and outdoor outlets and circuits call for ground-fault protection.
Cable that runs underground or along a fence needs the right type, buried or fastened the right way. These are the details that decide whether lights still work after the third winter.

sections.heading: LED and Controls
body: LED fixtures use less power and run cool, which lets you light more of the yard without loading up a circuit. We also handle LED retro-fits for fixtures you already have.
Controls matter as much as fixtures. A timer, a photocell or a switch inside the house means the lights come on when you want them, and not every night until someone remembers.

sections.heading: Add Outlets While We're There
body: If you're running power outside, it's a good time to ask for what you've been missing: an outlet on the patio for a string of lights or a grill, one at the shed, one on the back of the garage.
Extra outlets can go in on the same visit, at the house, the garage or the shed, when it makes sense for the job.
